prerequisites.answer: No. They are separate networks whose outputs share one space.

diagrams.title: Find an image using words
diagrams.subtitle: Shared space
trace: 1,000 CIFAR-10 test images are encoded once into a [1000, 512] table.
The query "a red sports car on a road" is tokenised and encoded into [1, 512].
Both tables are normalised, so a dot product is a cosine similarity.
One matrix product scores the query against every image: [1, 1000].
The six highest scores give the returned images.
diagrams.explanation: Text-to-image search uses two separate encoders that were trained to share one vector space. The gallery is encoded once into a table with one 512-number row per image. A query is tokenised and encoded into one 512-number vector. After normalisation, a single matrix product gives one similarity score per image, and the highest scores are returned. No caption is needed for the gallery images, and nothing is trained: the encoders are frozen.
diagrams.check_answer: No. Separate image and text encoders map into one shared space.
diagrams.notes:
In short: CLIP finds images for a text query by encoding both into one vector space and ranking images by similarity.

Explain: The gallery images pass through the image encoder once. The query passes through a separate text encoder. Both outputs are normalised 512-number vectors. A dot product then gives a cosine similarity for every image. The highest scores are the search results.

Example: 1,000 CIFAR-10 images become a [1000, 512] table. The query "a red sports car on a road" becomes [1, 512]. Multiplying the query by the transposed table gives [1, 1000] scores, and the top six are shown. A library catalogue is the analogy; books and requests use one shared set of subject codes.

Ask: Why encode the gallery only once?

Answer: Image vectors do not depend on the query, so they can be stored and reused for every search.

Watch out: The returned images are the closest matches, not proof that every word in the query is shown.

diagrams.insert_before_title: The contrastive objective as a matrix
diagrams.title: Score one batch of pairs
diagrams.subtitle: Matching diagonal
trace: With three pairs, S is [3, 3]; the diagonal holds the matching pairs.
Each row's softmax asks which caption matches that image.
Each column's softmax asks which image matches that caption.
Cross-entropy is low when the diagonal entry wins its row and its column.
The lab measures this loss on frozen embeddings; no optimiser runs.
diagrams.explanation: For a batch of N matching image–caption pairs, both encoders produce normalised vectors u and v. The score table S = u vᵀ / τ compares every image with every caption, so it is N × N, and the matching pairs lie on its diagonal. A row-wise softmax with cross-entropy asks each image to pick its own caption; the same on the transposed table asks each caption to pick its own image. CLIP averages the two losses. In the lab these losses are only measured on frozen embeddings.
diagrams.check_answer: On the diagonal: image i should match caption i, and caption i should match image i.
diagrams.notes:
In short: CLIP's loss scores every image against every caption in a batch and rewards the diagonal in both directions.

Explain: A batch holds N matching image–caption pairs. Encoding gives N image vectors u and N text vectors v. The score table S = u vᵀ / τ has one row per image and one column per caption. Row losses ask each image to pick its caption. Column losses ask each caption to pick its image.

Example: With three orthogonal pairs and τ = 1, each row is softmax([1, 0, 0]) ≈ [0.58, 0.21, 0.21]. The loss per row is −ln 0.58 ≈ 0.55, and the columns give the same. Shuffled captions move the high scores off the diagonal, so the loss rises.

Ask: Why compute the loss in both directions?

Answer: Search runs both ways, from images to captions and from captions to images, so both should be learned.

Watch out: The other captions in the batch act as negatives, even when one of them also describes the image well.

diagrams.title: Zero-shot classification route
diagrams.subtitle: No training; ten class texts
trace: Each of the 1,000 gallery images is encoded once.
Each class name fills one or more templates, such as "a photo of a cat."
The template vectors for a class are averaged and normalised again.
Every image is compared with the ten class vectors: a [N, 10] score table.
The highest score in each row is the predicted class; the labels only score the predictions.
diagrams.explanation: Zero-shot classification reuses the shared space. Each class name is placed into caption-like templates, encoded, averaged and normalised, giving ten class vectors. Each image vector is compared with all ten, and the most similar class is the prediction. The CIFAR-10 labels are used only to measure accuracy afterwards; no weights are trained on them. Changing the template wording changes the class vectors, so it can change both the predictions and the accuracy.
diagrams.check_answer: No. The labels are used only to score the predictions.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Zero-shot classification turns class names into caption vectors and gives each image the most similar class.

Explain: A template is caption wording with a slot for the class name. Several templates per class are encoded and averaged. The average is normalised again so its length is 1. Each image vector is compared with the ten class vectors. The highest score in each row is the prediction.

Example: "a photo of a cat." and "a blurry photo of a cat." are encoded and averaged into one cat vector. Ten class vectors form a [10, 512] table, and 1,000 images give a [1000, 10] score table. Accuracy is the fraction of rows whose highest score matches the label. A multiple-choice exam is the analogy; the options are written by us, not learned from this dataset.

Ask: Why normalise again after averaging?

Answer: An average of unit vectors is usually shorter than 1, which would scale every score for that class.

Watch out: A template that sounds unnatural to CLIP's training captions can lower accuracy without any model change.

diagrams.title: One contrastive training step
diagrams.subtitle: Original CLIP training
trace: CLIP trained on about 400 million image–caption pairs collected from the web.
Each batch of 32,768 pairs gave a 32,768 × 32,768 score table.
The symmetric loss rewarded matching pairs on the diagonal in both directions.
Gradients updated both encoders; the next batch repeated the step.
The lab never runs this update; it only measures the loss on six pairs.
diagrams.explanation: CLIP's original training repeated one contrastive step many times. A batch of web image–caption pairs passes through both encoders, every image is scored against every caption, and the symmetric cross-entropy rewards the matching pairs on the diagonal. Backpropagation then updates both encoders, pulling matching pairs together and pushing mismatched pairs apart. Large batches give many negatives per step. The lab measures this loss on frozen encoders but never performs the update.
diagrams.check_answer: No. It measures the loss on frozen embeddings; only the original training ran this loop.
diagrams.notes:
In short: CLIP was trained by repeating one step: score a batch of image–caption pairs, compute the symmetric loss, and update both encoders.

Explain: Each training batch contains matching image–caption pairs from the web. Both encoders produce vectors for every item. The score table compares every image with every caption. The symmetric loss rewards the diagonal in both directions. Gradients then update both encoders, and the next batch repeats the step.

Example: CLIP used about 400 million pairs and batches of 32,768, so each score table had over a billion entries. Each image competed against 32,767 wrong captions in its row. The lab uses six pairs and never updates the weights. Learning faces at a party is the analogy; every introduction also teaches who is not who.

Ask: Why do larger batches help contrastive training?

Answer: They provide more negative captions per image, which makes the matching task harder and more informative.

Watch out: Some "negatives" may describe the image well; contrastive training treats them as wrong anyway.

diagrams.title: Search a gallery using speech
diagrams.subtitle: Two models in a chain
trace: A spoken request is loaded as a 16,000-samples-per-second waveform.
Whisper converts it to a log-mel spectrogram and decodes words.
The transcript is encoded by CLIP's text encoder.
The query vector is compared with the stored gallery vectors.
The five highest-scoring images are returned; a misheard word changes them.
diagrams.explanation: Speech search chains two models. Whisper turns the audio into a transcript, and CLIP's text encoder turns that transcript into a query vector, which is compared with the stored gallery vectors. Each stage can be tested separately: word error rate measures the transcript, and precision@k measures the search. Because the image search sees only the transcript, any transcription error, and any information that is not words, such as tone, is lost before the search begins.
diagrams.check_answer: In the transcript: a misheard word changes the text query and so the ranking.
diagrams.notes:
In short: Speech search chains Whisper and CLIP: audio becomes text, text becomes a query vector, and the gallery is ranked.

Explain: Whisper is an encoder–decoder model for speech recognition. It reads a log-mel spectrogram and generates words. The transcript then goes to CLIP's text encoder. The query vector is compared with the stored image vectors. Word error rate measures the first stage separately.

Example: Suppose a speaker says "a red car" and Whisper hears "a bed car". The WER is 1/3, one substitution in three words. CLIP now searches for a bed car, and the top images may change. A relay race is the analogy; a dropped baton in the first leg slows every later runner.

Ask: What information is lost when speech becomes text?

Answer: Anything that is not words, such as tone, emotion, background sounds and who is speaking.

Watch out: Measure each stage on its own; a poor search result may come from the transcript, not from CLIP.

A score comparing two representations; larger means more similar here.

Precision@k counts relevant items in the top k; recall counts how many of all relevant items were found.

recap.title: What we learned: multimodal models
recap.question: High score proves a match?
recap.notes:
In short: Multimodal models turn different data types into comparable vectors, and every score still needs checking against the task.

Explain: Encoders map images, text and audio to vectors. Contrastive training aligns matching pairs in a shared space. Zero-shot classification compares images with class texts. Retrieval ranks images for a text query. Speech search adds a transcription stage measured by WER.

Example: In the lab, 1,000 images are encoded once and reused for classification, retrieval and the modality-gap plot. Precision@5 counts how many of the top five images match the query class. A transcript error changes the query before CLIP sees it.

Ask: Which single habit protects you most when using similarity scores?

Answer: Inspect the actual returned items and measure on labelled examples, rather than trusting the scores.

Watch out: Compare the stored GPU results with your CPU run only after naming their settings.

vocabulary_notes:
In short: Vectors, encoders and cosine similarity are the three ideas behind every result in today's lab.

Explain: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. An encoder is a network that turns an input into a vector. CLIP has one encoder for images and another for text. Cosine similarity compares the directions of two vectors. A high value means the two inputs are described similarly.

Example: The vectors [3, 4] and [4, 3] both have length 5. Their dot product is 12 + 12 = 24, so the cosine similarity is 24 ÷ 25 = 0.96. CLIP does the same with 512 numbers per vector. A compass bearing is an analogy; two walkers heading almost the same way have similar bearings, whatever their speeds.

Ask: Why divide by the two lengths?

Answer: So the score measures direction only; normalised vectors make the dot product the cosine directly.

Watch out: A cosine similarity is a match score, not a probability.
